42370:
Zechariah 2:10-4:7 (Hebrew 2:14-4:7) is the haftarah for the Sabbath of Hanukkah, because of the vision of the golden lampstand (menorah) and its key line, 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts' (Zech 4:6), which became the motto of the festival's meaning: God, not military strength, saves. The same passage is read with Beha'alotekha, where Aaron lights the lamps. Zechariah 14, with its picture of the nations going up each year to keep Sukkot in Jerusalem (Zech 14:16), is the haftarah for the first day of Sukkot.

Zechariah 14:9, 'On that day the LORD will be one and his name one', concludes the *Aleinu* prayer said at the end of every Jewish service, so Zechariah's hope for God's universal kingship closes Jewish worship daily. Zechariah 8:23, where ten men from the nations grasp the garment of a Jew saying 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you', has been read as the vision of Israel's priestly calling to the nations. The Talmud (*Sukkah* 52a) discusses the 'pierced one' of Zech 12:10, with one view applying it to the Messiah son of Joseph, a figure slain in the end-time war, showing that Jewish tradition also read the passage messianically.
42372: God calls the people not to repeat their ancestors' error: 'Return to me and I will return to you.'
42373: Visions assure that God is jealous for Jerusalem, will judge the nations, cleanse the priesthood and finish the temple by his Spirit.
42375: A crown for Joshua points to the Branch who will build the temple and bear royal honour.
42377: Asked about fasting, God answers: practise justice and mercy; then fasts will become feasts and nations will seek him.
42379: Zion's king rides in on a donkey, bringing peace to the nations, while worthless shepherds are judged.
42380: The pierced one and the fountain
42381: Jerusalem mourns the one it pierced; a fountain opens to cleanse sin; the shepherd is struck and the sheep scattered.
42383: The LORD stands on the Mount of Olives, living waters flow, and the nations worship at Sukkot.
42404: To call to mind and act on behalf of; it is the root of Zechariah's name ('the LORD remembers').
42405: Turning back to God, and God turning back to his people; the book's opening appeal.
42406: Passionate covenant zeal; God is jealous for Zion with great jealousy.
42408: A sprout from a stump; title for the coming Davidic ruler-priest.
42409: God's empowering presence, the source of the temple's completion, not human force.
42410: Haggai and Zechariah worked together on the temple project, addressing the same leaders in the same year.
42411: Matthew quotes the humble king on a donkey, the thirty pieces of silver and the struck shepherd in the passion story.
42412: John cites the king on a donkey and 'they will look on him whom they pierced' at the crucifixion.
42413: Revelation reuses Zechariah's horses, lampstands and olive trees, and the pierced one seen by all tribes.
42414: Ezekiel's river flowing from the temple and his shepherd oracles lie behind Zechariah's living waters and bad shepherds.
42415: Like Job, Zechariah shows 'the accuser' in the heavenly court, silenced by God.
42416: No prophetic book is quoted more densely in the Gospels' passion accounts. Jesus deliberately rides a donkey into Jerusalem, acting out Zech 9:9 (Matt 21:4-5; John 12:14-15). He applies 'strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered' to himself on the way to Gethsemane (Mark 14:27). Judas' thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field recall Zech 11:12-13 (Matt 27:9-10, where Matthew attributes it to Jeremiah, probably combining Jeremiah's field purchase with Zechariah). John sees the soldier's spear as 'they shall look on him whom they pierced' (John 19:37). Jesus' cleansing of the temple and his words on the Mount of Olives may also echo Zech 14 (Zech 14:21; Mark 11:15-17). Jewish interpretation reads these passages of Israel's future king, the Messiah son of David and (in one Talmudic view) a slain Messiah son of Joseph, and of a coming day when God reigns over all nations from Jerusalem.
42417: Zechariah 14 as a literal end-times map
42418: In popular prophecy teaching, Zech 14 is read as a precise script: a future siege of Jerusalem, Jesus' feet landing on the Mount of Olives which literally splits in two, and a millennial temple where nations keep the Feast of Tabernacles.
42419: Zechariah 9-14 uses apocalyptic imagery common in the late prophets: cosmic battle, a mountain split, living waters, a world with no night. Scholars such as Carol and Eric Meyers and Mark Boda read it as symbolic language for God's final victory, the purification of his people and the inclusion of the nations in Israel's worship. Jewish readers also read it as future but focus on God's universal kingship and the nations keeping Sukkot.
42420: Dispensational scholars (e.g. Charles Feinberg, Eugene Merrill) argue that the geographic detail (the Mount of Olives, specific gates) points to a literal future fulfilment at Christ's return, and note Acts 1:11-12 links Jesus' return with the Mount of Olives. Amillennial and many other evangelical scholars read it as symbolic of Christ's victory and the new creation. This is a genuine scholarly disagreement, not just a popular error.
42421: Whichever reading one holds, the chapter's main point, 'the LORD will be king over all the earth', should not be lost in arguments over timelines.
42422: A tiny, struggling community heard that God remembered them, had forgiven their priests, would finish the temple by his Spirit, and had a future in mind that included the nations. Later readers found in its shepherd oracles hope through times of failed leadership.
42423: Zechariah encourages people who feel small and overlooked: 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit'. It ties worship to justice and mercy, and points to a king who comes in humility and a day when the whole world is holy to God.
42424: In a series of arguments with a weary, cynical people, 'my messenger' defends God's covenant love, exposes careless worship, broken marriages and withheld tithes, and promises a messenger and Elijah before the great day.
42426: Either a prophet named Malachi or an anonymous prophet whose title was taken from Mal 3:1. The Greek Septuagint translates the heading as 'by the hand of his messenger'. Jewish tradition (Targum Jonathan on Mal 1:1; Talmud *Megillah* 15a, view of R. Joshua ben Korha) identifies Malachi with Ezra the scribe.
42427: Only the heading (Mal 1:1). The setting (a governor, a functioning temple, and the issues Nehemiah also faced) places the book in the mid-400s BC.
42428: The prophet addresses priests serving at the rebuilt temple.
42429: Priests and people of Judah in the Persian period
42431: Two or three generations after the return, the temple worked but the excitement was gone. Priests offered blind and lame animals, men divorced their Judean wives to marry outside the covenant, tithes went unpaid, and people asked where the God of justice was.
42433: Ezra arrives in Jerusalem (traditional date, in Artaxerxes I's seventh year) to teach the law.
42434: Nehemiah arrives as governor and rebuilds the walls.
42435: Nehemiah returns to find tithes neglected, priests compromised and mixed marriages (Neh 13).
42436: Letters from the Jewish garrison at Elephantine in Egypt show Judean life and temple concerns in the Persian empire.
42437:
By Malachi's time the prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah had not visibly come true. The temple stood, but there was no glory filling it, no Davidic king, no nations streaming in. Judah was still a small province under a Persian governor (Mal 1:8). Harvests were uncertain and locusts ('the devourer', Mal 3:11) a threat. The mood was tired and sceptical: 'It is vain to serve God' (Mal 3:14).

The problems Malachi names match those that Ezra and Nehemiah confronted. Nehemiah found the Levites had left the temple because their portions had not been paid (Neh 13:10-12), and men had married women from neighbouring peoples (Neh 13:23-27); a priestly family had married into Sanballat's household (Neh 13:28-29). Malachi adds that men were 'dealing treacherously' with the wives of their youth (Mal 2:14-16). Most scholars therefore date him around 460-430 BC, either just before or during Nehemiah's work.

The book is built from six disputations: God makes a statement, the people object ('How have you loved us?'), and God answers. This question-and-answer form lets the prophet expose the people's attitudes in their own words. The last verses, calling to remember Moses' law and promising Elijah, close the prophetic books in the Christian Old Testament and bridge to the Gospels.
42439: Each section quotes the people's objection ('How have we despised your name?') and answers it, a courtroom-style debate that turns their cynicism back on them.
42440: A son honours a father and a servant a master; offering God blind animals you would not give the governor shames him. Malachi frames worship in terms of honour owed in a relationship.
42442: Priests were meant to guard knowledge and teach Torah truly, as Levi's covenant required. Malachi's priests have corrupted that covenant by partiality.
42444: Malachi calls the wife 'your companion and your wife by covenant', with God as witness. Divorcing her to marry outside the covenant was treachery against both wife and God.
42446: Tithes (a tenth of produce) supported the Levites, priests and the poor; they were stored in temple storerooms. Withholding them starved the temple's ministry.
42448: Like a Persian king's record of loyal subjects (Esth 6:1-3), God keeps a scroll of those who fear him; they will be his treasured possession.
42449:
Malachi opens and closes with family love. 'I have loved you, says the LORD' (Mal 1:2) answers a people who doubted it; the end promises Elijah 'will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers' (Mal 4:6). Malachi 1:1-2:7 is the haftarah for parashat Toldot, where Jacob and Esau are born, because of 'I loved Jacob and hated Esau', which in its Hebrew idiom means choosing one for covenant role rather than personal hatred. Malachi 3:4-4:6 (Hebrew 3:4-24) is read on Shabbat HaGadol, the 'Great Sabbath' before Passover. Because the book ends with the word 'curse', the synagogue repeats the previous verse about Elijah so that the reading ends in hope.

The Elijah promise is central to Jewish expectation. At the Passover seder a cup is poured for Elijah and the door opened for him, the herald of redemption. In rabbinic tradition Elijah will resolve unsettled legal questions (the Talmud marks some debates teiku, 'let it stand' until Elijah comes) and restore families and peace (Mishnah *Eduyot* 8:7). Tradition counted Malachi with Haggai and Zechariah as the last of the prophets, after whom the holy spirit of prophecy departed from Israel. Malachi's call, 'Remember the Torah of my servant Moses' (Mal 4:4), shows the shift from prophetic voice to the study of Torah that shaped later Judaism.
42450: God affirms his covenant love for Jacob, shown against Edom's ruin; the people ask, 'How?'
42452: Priests offer blemished sacrifices and break Levi's covenant; God's name will be great among the nations.
42454: Marrying outside the covenant and divorcing the wife of one's youth profanes God's covenant.
42455: Where is the God of justice?
42456: God will send his messenger and come suddenly to his temple to refine priests and judge oppressors.
42458: Return to me; stop robbing God; test me and see blessings poured out.
42460: Against the cynics, a book of remembrance records the faithful; the day will burn the arrogant and heal the God-fearing.
42461: Keep the law of Moses; Elijah will come before the great day to turn hearts.
42466: It is vain to serve God
42483: Messenger or angel; the prophet's name/title and the coming herald who prepares God's way.
42484: A binding relationship with promises; Malachi speaks of covenants with Levi, the fathers, in marriage, and the 'messenger of the covenant'.
42486: To betray, to break faith; used five times in the marriage section.
42487: 'Return to me, and I will return to you': the covenant invitation, echoing Zechariah.
42489: Reverent awe and loyalty; those who fear God's name are remembered and healed.
42490: Nehemiah faced the same abuses: unpaid Levites, corrupted priests and mixed marriages.
42491: God's love for Jacob over Esau reaches back to the twins' story.
42492: Mark opens his Gospel by quoting Malachi's messenger (with Isaiah) for John the Baptist.
42493: Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah who was to come.
42494: The angel says John will go in the spirit and power of Elijah to turn fathers' hearts to their children.
42495: Paul quotes 'Jacob I loved, Esau I hated' in his discussion of God's election.
42496: The Gospels open where Malachi ends. Mark begins with Malachi's messenger who prepares the way (Mark 1:2), and the Gospels identify him as John the Baptist (Matt 11:10). Jesus says John is the 'Elijah who is to come' for those willing to accept it (Matt 11:14; Matt 17:12), while John himself denies being literally Elijah (John 1:21), so the fulfilment is in role and spirit (Luke 1:17). If John is the messenger, then the 'Lord who will suddenly come to his temple' (Mal 3:1) is Jesus, who enters the temple and cleanses it (Mark 11:15-17). Christians also read 'the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings' (Mal 4:2) of Christ, as in Charles Wesley's carol 'Hark! The Herald Angels Sing'. Jewish tradition still awaits Elijah as herald of the Messiah, honoured at every Passover seder and in the song 'Eliyahu ha-Navi' sung after Havdalah at the close of the Sabbath.
42497: Malachi 3:10 tithing as a prosperity formula
42498: Malachi 3:8-12 is widely preached as a guarantee: give ten percent of your income to your local church and God will open the windows of heaven and pour out financial blessing; fail to tithe and you are 'robbing God' and under a curse. Prosperity preachers extend it to 'seed faith' giving for returns.
42499: Malachi addresses an agricultural covenant community whose tithes of produce fed the Levites, priests and the poor (Deut 14:28-29; Neh 13:10-12). The blessing promised is rain and freedom from locusts so the land is fruitful (Mal 3:10-11), the covenant blessings of Deuteronomy for the nation. The 'curse' is the covenant curse on the whole people. Andrew Hill and Craig Blomberg stress that the passage is about covenant loyalty and supporting the temple's ministry, not an investment scheme for individuals.
42500: Many traditional evangelicals (e.g. R. T. Kendall) argue that tithing predates Moses (Gen 14:20; Gen 28:22) and remains a sound pattern, and that God does honour faithful, generous giving (2 Cor 9:6-11). Most evangelical scholars, however, including Blomberg and Hill, reject the prosperity reading as a misuse: New Testament giving is generous, cheerful and need-focused, and God's blessing is not a guaranteed financial return. On whether the tithe itself binds Christians, evangelicals genuinely disagree.
42501: Read as a formula, Malachi 3 can burden the poor and turn God into a vending machine; read in context it calls a community to honour God and provide for those who serve and those in need.
42502: 'I hate divorce' (Mal 2:16) as an absolute rule
42503: Mal 2:16, in older translations 'the LORD... saith that he hateth putting away', is often used to say that God hates all divorce, sometimes in ways that pressure victims of abuse or abandonment to stay.
42504: The Hebrew is difficult; many modern translations read 'the man who hates and divorces... covers his garment with violence' (ESV, similar NIV 2011). The context is men breaking faith with 'the wife of your youth' to marry outside the covenant. Gordon Hugenberger and David Instone-Brewer argue the verse condemns treacherous divorce that abandons a faithful wife, and links it with 'violence' against her.
42505: Traditional scholars (e.g. Joyce Baldwin, and many Reformed teachers) emphasise that whichever translation is right, the passage shows God's strong concern for marital faithfulness and the covenant witness of marriage. Most agree it should not be used to keep a spouse in an abusive situation, since the target of the condemnation is the unfaithful, violent partner.
42506: In context the verse protects the vulnerable spouse; it rebukes treachery and violence rather than adding burdens to those who are betrayed.
42507: For a weary community whose hopes seemed unfulfilled, Malachi insisted that God still loved them, that their worship, marriages and giving mattered to him, and that a day of justice and healing was coming, announced by a messenger.
42508: Malachi speaks to faith that has gone routine and cynical. It asks whether we give God our leftovers, keep faith with spouses, support those who serve and the poor, and still believe God will put things right. It also ends the Old Testament looking forward to someone who will prepare the way.
